title: Paediatrics
tagline: Growth and development, the newborn, immunisation, childhood illness and safeguarding
summary: Children are not small adults: their physiology, illnesses and needs change as they grow. This course covers growth and development, the newborn, immunisation, acute illness in childhood, congenital and genetic conditions, neurodevelopmental conditions, adolescent health and safeguarding.
overview: Paediatrics is not adult medicine at smaller doses. Children are still developing, so normal ranges, drug handling, immune responses and the pattern of illness all change with age. A fever in a 4-week-old baby is an emergency; the same temperature in a 9-year-old usually is not. This course teaches how to think about a patient who is a moving target.

The course starts with growth and development: how to measure a child, how to read a growth chart and how to recognise delay. It then follows the newborn through the transition at birth, the newborn examination, prematurity and jaundice, and explains the UK immunisation programme and how to talk with parents about vaccines. The chapter on acute illness teaches the structured assessment of the sick child, fever, dehydration and fluids, and the common respiratory emergencies.

Later chapters cover congenital heart disease, cystic fibrosis and chromosomal syndromes; autism, ADHD, cerebral palsy and learning disability; the adolescent consultation, confidentiality, mental health and transition to adult care; and safeguarding, from recognising abuse and neglect to the law and the multi-agency system that protects children.

Three habits run through every chapter: weigh the child before calculating a dose, plot the measurements before making a diagnosis, and treat the family as part of the clinical team. The course follows UK practice (NICE, UKHSA and RCPCH) and dates guidance that is likely to change.
outcomes: Measure and plot growth on UK-WHO and UK90 charts, calculate a mid-parental target height, and distinguish familial short stature and constitutional delay from pathological growth failure.
Describe developmental milestones by domain and age, recognise red flags such as regression, and outline developmental assessment and referral.
Explain the transition at birth and the newborn examination, and outline the recognition and management of neonatal jaundice, early-onset infection and the problems of preterm birth.

Explain how vaccines protect infants, set out the current UK routine immunisation schedule and its rationale, distinguish true from false contraindications, and respond to parental concerns with evidence.
Assess the acutely unwell child with a structured ABCDE approach and early-warning scores, use NICE traffic-light features in fever, and calculate weight-based maintenance fluids.
Recognise the presentations of congenital heart disease, cystic fibrosis and common chromosomal syndromes, and explain the principles of newborn screening.
Describe autism, ADHD, cerebral palsy and learning disability, their assessment and the educational, social and medical support around them.
Conduct a confidential consultation with a young person, assess competence to consent, and recognise eating disorders, depression, self-harm and substance use.
Recognise the physical and behavioural indicators of abuse and neglect, document findings, and describe the UK statutory framework for child protection.

history.title: A hospital for children
history.detail: Charles West opens the Hospital for Sick Children in Great Ormond Street, London, with ten beds. It becomes a model for children's hospitals and for paediatrics as a specialty.

history.title: Down syndrome described
history.detail: John Langdon Down describes the clinical features of the syndrome that now bears his name. In 1959 Jérôme Lejeune, Marthe Gautier and Raymond Turpin show that it is caused by an extra chromosome 21.

history.title: Incubators for premature babies
history.detail: The obstetrician Stéphane Tarnier introduces an incubator at the Paris Maternité, adapted from a poultry incubator. His colleague Pierre Budin later shows that warmth, feeding and hygiene improve the survival of premature babies.

history.title: School medical inspection
history.detail: The Education (Administrative Provisions) Act 1907 requires medical inspection of children in English elementary schools, a year after the Education (Provision of Meals) Act. Child health becomes a public service delivered at scale.

history.title: Attachment and maternal care
history.detail: John Bowlby's report for the World Health Organization, Maternal Care and Mental Health, argues that separation from the main carer harms young children. It changes hospital practice, including open visiting for parents.

history.title: The Apgar score
history.detail: Virginia Apgar proposes a simple score for assessing the newborn one minute after birth (published 1953). It is still used worldwide.

history.title: The battered-child syndrome
history.detail: C. Henry Kempe and colleagues describe the battered-child syndrome in JAMA. The paper leads to mandatory reporting laws in the United States and to the modern recognition of child abuse.

history.title: British growth standards
history.detail: James Tanner, R. H. Whitehouse and Michio Takaishi publish British growth standards for height, weight and velocity. Measuring and plotting growth becomes routine at every child health contact.

history.title: Surfactant for respiratory distress
history.detail: Building on John Clements's work on lung surfactant and Mary Ellen Avery and Jere Mead's 1959 finding that it is deficient in respiratory distress syndrome, Tetsuro Fujiwara reports successful treatment of preterm babies with artificial surfactant.

history.title: WHO Child Growth Standards
history.detail: The World Health Organization publishes growth standards based on healthy breastfed children in six countries. In 2009 the UK adopts them for children under 4 as the UK-WHO growth charts.
